tool.name: Streamlit
tool.tagline: Turn Python scripts into interactive data apps with no front-end code
tool.description: Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for building interactive web apps for data, machine learning and internal tools. You write a plain script with calls like st.slider and st.dataframe; Streamlit reruns it on every interaction and renders the result in the browser, with caching, session state, multipage navigation and chat elements built in.

concepts.name: Scripts that rerun: the execution model
concepts.summary: A Streamlit app is a Python script that reruns from top to bottom every time a user interacts with it.
concepts.why: Every Streamlit design decision, from caching to session state, follows from this one rule.
concepts.body:
A Streamlit app is an ordinary Python file. Start it with:

```bash
pip install streamlit
streamlit run app.py
```

Streamlit starts a local web server (by default on `http://localhost:8501`) and opens the browser. Calls such as `st.title`, `st.write` and `st.slider` add elements to the page in the order they run.

The central idea is the **rerun model**: whenever a user changes a widget (moves a slider, clicks a button, types text), Streamlit runs your **entire script again from the top**. This time, the widget call returns the new value, so the code below it computes and displays updated results. There are no callbacks or event handlers required for the basic case: you write straight-line code and Streamlit handles the rest.

Consequences to keep in mind:

- Ordinary variables are reset on every rerun; anything you need to remember goes in `st.session_state`.
- Slow work (loading a big file, calling an API, training a model) would repeat on every click, so you cache it with `@st.cache_data` or `@st.cache_resource`.
- Each browser tab is a separate **session** with its own reruns and state.

While developing, saving the file makes the app offer to rerun ("Always rerun" reruns automatically on every save), giving a fast edit-and-see loop. `streamlit hello` runs a built-in demo to check your installation.
concepts.code:
# app.py  -> start with:  streamlit run app.py
import time
import streamlit as st

st.title("Rerun demo")
n = st.slider("How many squares?", 1, 10, 3)   # returns the current value

st.write("Script ran at", time.strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
st.write("Squares:", [i * i for i in range(n)])

clicks = 0            # plain variables reset on every rerun...
if st.button("Click me"):
    clicks += 1
st.write("clicks =", clicks)   # ...so this never goes above 1
# Moving the slider reruns the whole script: the time and n both change.
takeaways: `streamlit run app.py` serves the script as a web app
Every widget interaction reruns the whole script top to bottom
Plain variables reset each rerun; use session state and caching for memory and speed
pitfalls: Expecting a normal variable to keep its value between interactions.

quiz.q: A user moves a slider in a Streamlit app. What happens?
options: Only the slider's callback function runs
Nothing until the user presses Submit
The whole script runs again from the top, with the slider returning its new value
The page reloads and resets all widgets
quiz.explain: Streamlit reruns the entire script on each interaction; widget calls return their current values.

concepts.name: Displaying text, data and metrics
concepts.summary: Show text, Markdown, DataFrames, metrics, JSON and code with st.write and the dedicated display elements.
concepts.why: Most apps are mainly displaying results, and choosing the right element makes them readable at a glance.
concepts.body:
**`st.write`** is the Swiss Army knife: it accepts strings (rendered as Markdown), numbers, DataFrames, dicts, figures and more, and picks a suitable display. It also takes several arguments: `st.write("Total:", total)`.

**Magic**: a bare expression on its own line, such as a variable name or a string, is written to the app automatically, as if wrapped in `st.write`. Handy for quick scripts; explicit calls are clearer in larger apps.

Dedicated elements give more control:

- Text: `st.title`, `st.header`, `st.subheader`, `st.markdown` (with emoji shortcodes and colored text like `:blue[text]`), `st.caption`, `st.code(src, language="python")`, `st.latex`.
- Data: `st.dataframe(df)` is an interactive grid with sorting, search and column resizing; `column_config` formats columns (currency, progress bars, links, images). `st.table` renders a static table. `st.json` shows a collapsible tree.
- KPIs: `st.metric("Revenue", "$12.3k", "+4.5%")` shows a value with a colored delta.
- Status: `st.success`, `st.info`, `st.warning`, `st.error`, `st.exception`, and `st.toast` for brief notifications.

`st.dataframe` handles large frames efficiently, but sending millions of rows to the browser is still slow; filter or aggregate first.

Anything displayed is part of the page only until the next rerun, when the script redraws everything from scratch.
concepts.code:
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

df = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["Tea", "Coffee", "Cocoa"],
                   "revenue": [1200.5, 3400.0, 560.25],
                   "share": [0.23, 0.66, 0.11]})

st.title("Sales overview")
st.markdown("Revenue for **March**, :blue[all regions].")

col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
col1.metric("Revenue", f"${df.revenue.sum():,.0f}", "+4.5%")
col2.metric("Products", len(df), "-1")

st.dataframe(df, hide_index=True, column_config={
    "revenue": st.column_config.NumberColumn("Revenue", format="$%.2f"),
    "share": st.column_config.ProgressColumn("Share", min_value=0, max_value=1),
})
st.write("Top product:", df.loc[df.revenue.idxmax(), "product"])
"Magic: this bare string is displayed too"
st.success("Data loaded")
takeaways: `st.write` displays almost anything; bare expressions are shown via magic
`st.dataframe` with `column_config` gives interactive, formatted tables
`st.metric` shows KPIs with deltas; status elements show messages
pitfalls: Sending a multi-million-row DataFrame to `st.dataframe` instead of filtering or aggregating first.

quiz.q: What does a line containing only a variable name, such as `df`, do in a Streamlit script?
options: Displays it, as if passed to st.write (magic)
quiz.explain: Streamlit magic writes bare expressions to the app automatically.

concepts.name: Input widgets
concepts.summary: Collect user input with buttons, sliders, text inputs, select boxes and file uploaders, and understand what each returns.
concepts.why: Widgets are how users drive an app, and their return values feed the rest of the script.
concepts.body:
Each widget call draws a control **and returns its current value**:

- `st.button("Run")` returns `True` only during the rerun triggered by the click, then `False` again.
- `st.checkbox`, `st.toggle` return booleans.
- `st.slider("Age", 0, 100, 25)` returns a number, or a tuple for a range with `value=(20, 40)`.
- `st.number_input`, `st.text_input`, `st.text_area`, `st.date_input`, `st.time_input`.
- `st.selectbox`, `st.radio`, `st.segmented_control` return one option; `st.multiselect` and `st.pills` (with `selection_mode="multi"`) return lists.
- `st.file_uploader` returns an uploaded file object (or `None`), readable with `pd.read_csv(file)`.
- `st.download_button` lets users download data you generate.

Common parameters: `help=` adds a tooltip, `disabled=`, `placeholder=`, `label_visibility="collapsed"`, `format_func=` to show nicer labels for options, and `key=` to give the widget an explicit identity.

Streamlit identifies a widget by its parameters (label, options, ...) or by its `key`. Two widgets with identical parameters raise a `DuplicateWidgetID` error; give them different keys. Changing a widget's label or options between reruns can reset it to its default, because Streamlit sees a new widget.

Since `st.button` is only `True` for one rerun, things shown "after clicking" disappear on the next interaction. Store the result in session state if it must persist.
concepts.code:
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

name = st.text_input("Your name", placeholder="Ada")
plan = st.selectbox("Plan", ["free", "pro", "team"], index=1,
                    format_func=str.title, help="Billing plan")
seats = st.slider("Seats", 1, 50, 5, disabled=(plan == "free"))
extras = st.multiselect("Extras", ["SSO", "Audit log", "Support"])
upload = st.file_uploader("Usage CSV", type="csv")

price = {"free": 0, "pro": 12, "team": 20}[plan] * seats + 15 * len(extras)
st.write(f"Hi {name or 'there'}, your monthly price is ${price}")

if upload is not None:
    st.dataframe(pd.read_csv(upload).head())

if st.button("Confirm"):          # True only on the rerun caused by the click
    st.success("Order placed")
st.download_button("Download quote", f"price={price}\n", file_name="quote.txt")
takeaways: Widgets return their current value on every rerun
`st.button` is True only for the rerun its click caused
Widgets are identified by parameters or `key`; duplicates need distinct keys
pitfalls: Putting results inside `if st.button(...)` and expecting them to stay visible after the next interaction.

quiz.q: You create two `st.text_input('Email')` widgets in the same app. What happens?
options: Both share the same value automatically
Streamlit raises a duplicate widget ID error unless they get different keys
quiz.explain: Widgets with identical parameters get the same ID; give each a unique key.

concepts.name: Charts and maps
concepts.summary: Display charts with Streamlit's built-in chart elements or with Matplotlib, Plotly, Altair and other libraries.
concepts.why: Visual results are the heart of most data apps, and Streamlit renders the libraries you already know.
concepts.body:
Streamlit has quick **built-in charts** that take a DataFrame and need no plotting library code:

- `st.line_chart(df, x="date", y=["a", "b"])`
- `st.area_chart`, `st.bar_chart` (with `horizontal=True` or `stack=False`), `st.scatter_chart`
- `st.map(df)` plots points from `lat`/`lon` (or `latitude`/`longitude`) columns on a map

They are built on Altair and are interactive (hover, zoom), but offer limited customization.

For full control, render a figure from your plotting library:

- `st.plotly_chart(fig)`: interactive Plotly figures; with `on_select="rerun"` it returns the user's selected points.
- `st.altair_chart(chart)` and `st.vega_lite_chart`.
- `st.pyplot(fig)`: Matplotlib and seaborn figures as static images. Pass the figure object explicitly instead of relying on global pyplot state, which is shared between sessions.
- `st.pydeck_chart` for advanced 3D maps, `st.graphviz_chart` for graphs.

Charts stretch to the container width by default; use `width=` and `height=` to size them, and put them inside columns or tabs for layout.

Because the script reruns on each interaction, chart code reruns too. Build figures from cached data so redrawing stays fast, and avoid generating heavy Matplotlib figures for every keystroke in a text input.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import streamlit as st

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
df = pd.DataFrame({"day": pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=60),
                   "visits": rng.poisson(200, 60).cumsum(),
                   "signups": rng.poisson(20, 60).cumsum()})

st.line_chart(df, x="day", y=["visits", "signups"])        # built-in

fig = px.scatter(df, x="visits", y="signups", title="Visits vs signups")
st.plotly_chart(fig)                                       # interactive

mfig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(np.diff(df.visits), bins=15)
st.pyplot(mfig)                                            # static image

pts = pd.DataFrame({"lat": [59.91, 48.86], "lon": [10.75, 2.35]})
st.map(pts, zoom=3)
takeaways: Built-in `st.line_chart`, `bar_chart`, `scatter_chart` and `map` take DataFrames directly
`st.plotly_chart`, `st.altair_chart` and `st.pyplot` render library figures
Pass Matplotlib figure objects explicitly to `st.pyplot`
pitfalls: Calling `st.pyplot()` with no figure, relying on pyplot's global state shared across users.

quiz.q: You need hover tooltips, zoom and the ability to read which points a user lasso-selected. Which element fits?
quiz.explain: Plotly charts are interactive and on_select returns the selected points to Python.

concepts.name: Layout: sidebar, columns, tabs and containers
concepts.summary: Arrange elements with the sidebar, columns, tabs, expanders, containers and placeholders, and configure the page.
concepts.why: A clear layout separates controls from results and keeps dense apps readable.
concepts.body:
By default elements stack vertically in the main area. Layout primitives change that:

- **Sidebar**: `st.sidebar.selectbox(...)`, or `with st.sidebar:` for a block. Ideal for filters and settings.
- **Columns**: `left, right = st.columns(2)` or relative widths `st.columns([3, 1])`; `gap=` and `vertical_alignment=` adjust spacing.
- **Tabs**: `tab1, tab2 = st.tabs(["Chart", "Data"])`. All tabs' content is computed on each rerun, only display is switched, so expensive tabs still cost time.
- **Expander**: `with st.expander("Details"):` hides secondary content.
- **Popover**: `with st.popover("Settings"):` a button that opens a small floating panel.
- **Container**: `st.container(border=True)` groups elements, and lets you write into a region later in the script: create it early, fill it later.
- **Placeholder**: `slot = st.empty()` holds a single element you can replace, such as progress text updated in a loop.

Every layout object supports both styles: `col.write(...)` and `with col: st.write(...)`.

`st.set_page_config(page_title="Sales", page_icon="📈", layout="wide")` sets the browser tab title and icon and switches to full-width layout; call it near the top of the script.

Nesting is allowed (columns inside tabs, containers in columns), but deep nesting gets cramped on small screens. Columns stack vertically on narrow mobile displays.
concepts.code:
import streamlit as st

st.set_page_config(page_title="Dashboard", layout="wide")

with st.sidebar:
    region = st.selectbox("Region", ["EU", "US", "APAC"])
    show_raw = st.toggle("Show raw data")

header = st.container()               # reserve space at the top, fill it later
left, right = st.columns([3, 1], vertical_alignment="center")
left.subheader(f"Sales in {region}")
right.metric("Orders", 1280, "+3%")

chart_tab, data_tab = st.tabs(["Chart", "Data"])
with chart_tab:
    st.bar_chart({"Q1": [10], "Q2": [14], "Q3": [12]})
with data_tab:
    if show_raw:
        st.write({"Q1": 10, "Q2": 14, "Q3": 12})

with st.expander("Methodology"):
    st.write("Orders are counted at shipping time.")
header.info(f"Filters: region={region}")   # appears above the columns
takeaways: Sidebar for controls, columns and tabs for side-by-side or alternative views
Containers and `st.empty()` let you fill or replace regions later
`st.set_page_config(layout='wide')` uses the full browser width
pitfalls: Putting slow computations in a tab assuming they only run when the tab is opened; all tabs run every rerun.

quiz.q: A dashboard has an expensive chart in the third tab. When is it computed?
options: On every rerun, because all tab contents run regardless of which is visible
Only when the user opens that tab
quiz.explain: Tabs only switch visibility; the script still executes the code inside every tab.

concepts.name: Caching with st.cache_data and st.cache_resource
concepts.summary: Avoid repeating slow work on every rerun by caching data results and shared resources, with TTLs and invalidation.
concepts.why: Without caching, every click reloads data and recomputes everything, making apps slow and expensive.
concepts.body:
Because scripts rerun constantly, caching is essential. Streamlit offers two decorators.

**`@st.cache_data`** caches the **return value** of a function keyed by its arguments (and its source code). Use it for anything that produces data: reading files, querying a database, calling an API, transforming DataFrames.

- Each call returns a **copy** of the cached value, so callers can mutate the result safely.
- The value must be pickleable.
- `ttl="1h"` expires entries, essential for data that changes; `max_entries=` bounds memory.
- Arguments must be hashable by Streamlit; prefix a parameter with an underscore (`_conn`) to exclude it from the key.

**`@st.cache_resource`** caches **one shared object**, without copying, for things that should exist once per server: database connections, ML models, API clients.

- All sessions get the same object, so it must be thread-safe, and mutating it affects every user.

Both caches are **global**: shared across all users and sessions of the app process, which makes them efficient but means never caching user-specific secrets under a key other users can hit.

Invalidate with `my_func.clear()` for one function, or `st.cache_data.clear()` for all. Editing the function's code also invalidates its cache.

Pick by the question "is this data or a connection/model?": DataFrames and results go to `cache_data`; live objects go to `cache_resource`.
takeaways: `cache_data` caches return values per argument set and returns copies
`cache_resource` caches one shared, uncopied object such as a connection or model
Use `ttl` for changing data and `.clear()` to invalidate
pitfalls: Using cache_resource for a DataFrame that callers then mutate, changing it for every user.

quiz.q: Which decorator fits a database connection pool used by every session?
quiz.explain: Connections are shared live resources, which cache_resource stores once without copying.

concepts.name: Session state and callbacks
concepts.summary: Keep values across reruns with st.session_state, link it to widget keys, and react to changes with on_change and on_click callbacks.
concepts.why: Counters, multi-step flows, chat histories and any app that remembers anything depend on session state.
concepts.body:
`st.session_state` is a dictionary-like object that **persists across reruns** for one user session (one browser tab). Use attribute or key syntax:

```python
if "count" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.count = 0
st.session_state.count += 1
```

Always initialize keys before use, because the first run starts empty.

**Widgets and state are linked**: a widget with `key="city"` stores its value in `st.session_state.city`. You can read it anywhere, and you can set it before the widget is created to change the widget programmatically. Setting it after the widget was created in the same run raises an error.

**Callbacks** run before the rerun's script, which makes state updates take effect immediately:

```python
st.button("+1", on_click=increment, args=(1,))
st.text_input("Name", key="name", on_change=normalize_name)
```

Without a callback, `if st.button(...): st.session_state.count += 1` updates the state *after* any earlier lines have already displayed the old value, a common source of "off by one click" bugs.

Session state is per tab: a page refresh or a new tab starts a new, empty session. For data that must survive restarts or be shared between users, use a database or file, not session state.

Widget values are removed from session state when the widget is not rendered in a run (for example on another page), so copy values you need to keep into your own keys.
concepts.code:
import streamlit as st

if "count" not in st.session_state:          # initialize once per session
    st.session_state.count = 0
    st.session_state.history = []

def add(step):                               # callback: runs before the script
    st.session_state.count += step
    st.session_state.history.append(step)

def shout():
    st.session_state.name = st.session_state.name.upper()

st.button("+1", on_click=add, args=(1,))
st.button("+10", on_click=add, args=(10,))
st.write("Count:", st.session_state.count)   # already updated: no lag
st.write("Steps:", st.session_state.history)

st.text_input("Name", key="name", on_change=shout)   # value lives in state
st.write("Stored:", st.session_state.get("name", ""))
takeaways: `st.session_state` persists values across reruns within one browser tab
Widget `key`s map widget values into session state
Callbacks (`on_click`, `on_change`) update state before the script reruns
pitfalls: Updating state inside `if st.button(...)` after the value was already displayed, so the page lags one click behind.

quiz.q: A user refreshes the browser page. What happens to st.session_state?
options: It is reset: a refresh starts a new session
It is shared with other users
It is saved to disk automatically
quiz.explain: Session state lives in the server session for that tab; a refresh creates a new session.

concepts.name: Forms: batching input
concepts.summary: Group widgets in st.form so the app reruns only when the user submits, not on every change.
concepts.why: Forms stop expensive reruns while users fill several fields, and match how people expect to enter data.
concepts.body:
Normally each widget change triggers a rerun. Inside **`st.form`**, widget changes are held in the browser until the user clicks the form's **submit button**; then the script reruns once with all the new values.

```python
with st.form("signup"):
    email = st.text_input("Email")
    plan = st.radio("Plan", ["free", "pro"])
    submitted = st.form_submit_button("Sign up")
if submitted:
    save(email, plan)
```

Rules:

- Every form needs at least one `st.form_submit_button`; Streamlit shows an error otherwise.
- Ordinary `st.button` and `st.download_button` are not allowed inside forms.
- Only the submit button can have a callback inside a form; widgets inside cannot use `on_change`. Use `on_click` on the submit button, which runs before the rerun with all form values available in session state (via keys).
- `clear_on_submit=True` resets the inputs after a submission, useful for entry forms.
- `enter_to_submit` controls whether pressing Enter in a text field submits.

Before submission, widget return values are their previous (or default) values, so read values in the `if submitted:` branch.

Forms are ideal when inputs only make sense together (a search with several filters, a record to save), or when each rerun is expensive. For instant feedback on every change, use plain widgets.
concepts.code:
import streamlit as st

if "orders" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.orders = []

def place_order():                     # submit callback: values are in state
    s = st.session_state
    s.orders.append({"item": s.item, "qty": s.qty, "rush": s.rush})

with st.form("order", clear_on_submit=True):
    st.selectbox("Item", ["Tea", "Coffee", "Cocoa"], key="item")
    st.number_input("Quantity", min_value=1, max_value=20, value=1, key="qty")
    st.checkbox("Rush delivery", key="rush")
    submitted = st.form_submit_button("Place order", on_click=place_order)

if submitted:
    st.success(f"Order #{len(st.session_state.orders)} placed")
st.write(st.session_state.orders)
# Changing the inputs does not rerun the app; only clicking the button does.
takeaways: Widgets inside `st.form` only trigger a rerun when the form is submitted
Each form needs a `st.form_submit_button`; only it may have a callback
Read values after submission, or in the submit callback via keys
pitfalls: Adding `on_change` callbacks to widgets inside a form, which Streamlit does not allow.

quiz.q: A form has five inputs. How many reruns happen when a user edits all five and clicks submit once?
quiz.explain: Inside a form, changes are batched in the browser and sent together on submit, causing one rerun.

concepts.name: Multipage apps with st.navigation
concepts.summary: Split an app into pages with st.Page and st.navigation, group them in sections, and link or switch between pages.
concepts.why: Real apps grow beyond one screen; structured navigation keeps code and UI organized.
concepts.body:
The recommended way to build multipage apps is an **entrypoint file** that defines pages and calls `st.navigation`:

```python
pg = st.navigation([
    st.Page("pages/dashboard.py", title="Dashboard", icon=":material/dashboard:"),
    st.Page("pages/settings.py", title="Settings"),
])
pg.run()
```

`st.Page` accepts a file path or a **function**, so small pages can live in one file. Pass a dict to group pages into sections: `{"Reports": [...], "Admin": [...]}`. `position="top"` puts navigation in a top bar instead of the sidebar. `default=True` marks the home page, and `url_path=` sets the page's URL.

The entrypoint runs on every rerun before the page, so it is the place for shared things: `st.set_page_config`, login checks, common sidebar widgets and building the page list. Because the list is built in code, you can show admin pages only to admins.

Move between pages with `st.page_link(page, label=...)` (a link) or `st.switch_page(page)` (programmatic, for example after a form submits).

Session state is shared across pages within a session, so a selection made on one page can be used on another. Widget values themselves are cleaned up when their page is not shown; copy what you need into your own state keys.

The older convention, a `pages/` directory next to the main script that Streamlit turns into pages automatically, still works but offers less control.
concepts.code:
# streamlit_app.py  (entrypoint)
import streamlit as st

def home():
    st.title("Home")
    st.page_link(settings, label="Go to settings", icon=":material/settings:")

def settings():
    st.title("Settings")
    st.session_state.theme = st.radio("Theme", ["light", "dark"])

def admin():
    st.title("Admin")

home_page = st.Page(home, title="Home", icon=":material/home:", default=True)
settings = st.Page(settings, title="Settings")
pages = {"App": [home_page, settings]}
if st.session_state.get("is_admin"):            # pages can depend on the user
    pages["Admin"] = [st.Page(admin, title="Admin")]

st.set_page_config(page_title="My app")
pg = st.navigation(pages, position="sidebar")
pg.run()
takeaways: Define pages with `st.Page` and run the selected one via `st.navigation(...).run()`
The entrypoint runs every rerun: put shared config, auth and widgets there
Navigate with `st.page_link` or `st.switch_page`; session state is shared across pages
pitfalls: Forgetting to call `.run()` on the page returned by `st.navigation`, so no page content appears.

quiz.q: Where should a login check that protects every page go in an st.navigation app?
options: In the entrypoint file, before calling st.navigation(...).run()
quiz.explain: The entrypoint runs on every rerun before any page, so checks there cover all pages.

concepts.name: Secrets and data connections
concepts.summary: Store credentials in secrets.toml, read them with st.secrets, and query databases and APIs with st.connection.
concepts.why: Real apps talk to databases and APIs, and credentials must never end up in the code or the repository.
concepts.body:
**Secrets** go in `.streamlit/secrets.toml` (in the project or `~/.streamlit/`), written in TOML:

```toml
api_key = "sk-..."
[connections.warehouse]
url = "postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db"
```

Read them with `st.secrets["api_key"]` or `st.secrets.connections.warehouse.url`. Root-level keys are also exposed as environment variables. Add `secrets.toml` to `.gitignore`; on Streamlit Community Cloud and other hosts you paste secrets into the platform's settings instead.

**`st.connection`** creates a cached, configured connection from those secrets:

```python
conn = st.connection("warehouse", type="sql")
df = conn.query("select * from sales where region = :r", params={"r": region}, ttl="10m")
```

- `type="sql"` uses SQLAlchemy and needs a driver for your database; `type="snowflake"` is also built in, and third-party packages provide others.
- `query` results are cached with `st.cache_data` under the hood; `ttl` controls freshness.
- The connection object itself is cached as a resource, created once per app process.
- Use bound parameters (`:r`) instead of f-strings to avoid SQL injection.

For services without a connection class, read the key from `st.secrets` and create your client inside an `@st.cache_resource` function.

Secrets are server-side only: they never reach the browser unless you display them. Be careful not to `st.write(st.secrets)` while debugging a deployed app.
concepts.code:
# .streamlit/secrets.toml (never commit this file):
#   api_key = "demo-key"
#   [connections.shop]
#   url = "sqlite:///shop.db"
import streamlit as st

conn = st.connection("shop", type="sql")      # reads [connections.shop]

region = st.selectbox("Region", ["EU", "US"])
df = conn.query("select :r as region, 42 as amount",
                params={"r": region}, ttl="10m")   # cached per params
st.dataframe(df)

key = st.secrets["api_key"]                   # use it, never display it
st.write("API key loaded:", bool(key))
takeaways: Keep credentials in `.streamlit/secrets.toml` (git-ignored) and read via `st.secrets`
`st.connection(name, type='sql')` builds a cached connection from secrets
`conn.query(..., params=..., ttl=...)` caches results and avoids SQL injection
pitfalls: Committing secrets.toml to Git, or formatting user input directly into SQL strings.

quiz.q: How does `conn.query(sql, ttl='10m')` avoid hitting the database on every rerun?
options: Its results are cached (via st.cache_data) for 10 minutes per query and params
It opens a new connection each time
It stores results in session state
It does not; every rerun queries again
quiz.explain: query wraps the call in Streamlit's data cache, keyed by SQL and parameters, expiring after ttl.

concepts.name: Fragments, dialogs and controlling reruns
concepts.summary: Rerun only part of a page with st.fragment, refresh it on a timer, open modal dialogs, and trigger reruns with st.rerun.
concepts.why: Full-script reruns get slow in big apps; fragments make interactions local and enable live-updating panels.
concepts.body:
A **fragment** is a function decorated with `@st.fragment`. When a widget *inside* the fragment changes, Streamlit reruns **only that function**, not the whole script. Widgets outside still trigger full reruns.

```python
@st.fragment
def filters_and_chart():
    metric = st.radio("Metric", ["visits", "signups"])
    st.line_chart(load_data()[metric])
```

Use fragments for self-contained parts of a page: a chart with its own controls, a form-like panel, a table editor. Pass `run_every="10s"` to rerun the fragment on a timer, which gives live dashboards without a full page refresh.

Things to know:

- Values computed inside a fragment are not visible to the rest of the script until a full rerun; share them via session state.
- A fragment's elements are redrawn in place on each fragment rerun. Its widgets must be drawn in its own body, not into containers created outside it.
- `st.rerun()` triggers an immediate rerun of the whole app; inside a fragment, `st.rerun(scope="fragment")` reruns just the fragment.

**Dialogs** are fragments shown as a modal: decorate a function with `@st.dialog("Title")` and call it, typically from a button. Widgets inside the dialog rerun only the dialog; call `st.rerun()` to close it and refresh the app once the user confirms.

`st.stop()` ends the current run immediately, useful for guards such as "please upload a file first".
takeaways: `@st.fragment` reruns only that function when its own widgets change
`run_every` refreshes a fragment on a timer for live views
`@st.dialog` builds modals; `st.rerun()` and `st.stop()` control execution
pitfalls: Expecting values computed inside a fragment to update the rest of the page without a full rerun.

quiz.q: Inside `@st.fragment def panel():` a user moves a slider that belongs to the fragment. What reruns?
quiz.explain: Widget interactions inside a fragment rerun just that fragment.

concepts.name: Chat and LLM apps
concepts.summary: Build conversational interfaces with st.chat_message, st.chat_input and st.write_stream, keeping history in session state.
concepts.why: Chat front ends for LLMs and assistants are one of the most common things people build with Streamlit.
concepts.body:
Streamlit has elements made for chat interfaces:

- `st.chat_input("Ask something")` renders an input pinned to the bottom of the page and returns the submitted text (or `None`) for the rerun after the user presses Enter. It can also accept file attachments with `accept_file=True`.
- `with st.chat_message("user"):` (or `"assistant"`, or any name with an `avatar=`) draws a message bubble; anything written inside appears in it.
- `st.write_stream(generator)` writes a stream of text chunks as they arrive, with a typewriter effect, and returns the full concatenated text when done. It accepts plain generators and the streaming responses of OpenAI-style clients.

Because the script reruns on every message, the conversation must live in **session state**. The standard pattern:

1. Initialize `st.session_state.messages = []`.
2. Re-display every stored message at the top of each run.
3. When `chat_input` returns text, display it, call the model, stream the reply, and append both messages to the history.

Cache the model client with `@st.cache_resource`, and read API keys from `st.secrets`.

`st.status("Thinking...")` shows expandable progress for multi-step agents, and `st.feedback("thumbs")` collects ratings. Long conversations cost tokens and memory: trim or summarize history before sending it to the model.
concepts.code:
import time
import streamlit as st

def fake_llm(prompt):                  # stand-in for a streaming LLM call
    for word in f"You said: {prompt}. Nice!".split():
        yield word + " "
        time.sleep(0.05)

if "messages" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.messages = [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi! Ask me anything."}]

for m in st.session_state.messages:    # redraw history on every rerun
    with st.chat_message(m["role"]):
        st.markdown(m["content"])

if prompt := st.chat_input("Your message"):
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})
    with st.chat_message("user"):
        st.markdown(prompt)
    with st.chat_message("assistant"):
        reply = st.write_stream(fake_llm(prompt))   # returns the full text
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
takeaways: `st.chat_input` returns the submitted message; `st.chat_message` draws bubbles
Keep the conversation in session state and redraw it every run
`st.write_stream` displays streamed tokens and returns the full reply
pitfalls: Not storing messages in session state, so the conversation disappears on the next message.

quiz.q: Why does a Streamlit chat app loop over `st.session_state.messages` at the top of the script?
options: To send them to the model again
Because each rerun starts with an empty page, so history must be redrawn
quiz.explain: Reruns redraw everything from scratch; stored history is displayed again each time.

concepts.name: Testing apps with AppTest
concepts.summary: Write fast, headless tests for Streamlit apps with streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest and pytest.
concepts.why: Automated tests catch broken widgets and logic before users do, without clicking through the app by hand.
concepts.body:
`streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest` runs an app script **without a browser** and lets you inspect and interact with its elements:

```python
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest
at = AppTest.from_file("app.py").run()
```

`from_string` and `from_function` create apps from code directly, handy for small tests. After `.run()`:

- Elements are accessed by type, as lists in order of appearance: `at.title[0].value`, `at.markdown`, `at.metric`, `at.dataframe`, `at.error`, `at.exception`.
- Widgets are accessed the same way or by key: `at.slider[0]`, `at.text_input(key="name")`.
- Interact, then run again: `at.slider[0].set_value(5).run()`, `at.button[0].click().run()`, `at.text_input[0].input("Ada").run()`, `at.selectbox[0].select("pro").run()`.
- `at.session_state["count"]` reads or presets state; `at.secrets["api_key"] = "test"` provides secrets.
- `at.switch_page("pages/admin.py")` tests multipage apps.

Assert that no exception occurred with `assert not at.exception`. Tests run in a fresh session each time, so they are isolated and fast enough for CI with pytest.

AppTest does not render HTML or JavaScript, so it cannot test visual layout or custom components; for that, use browser tests (Playwright). Keep business logic in plain functions with their own unit tests and use AppTest for the wiring.
concepts.code:
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

def app():                              # the app under test
    import streamlit as st
    price = st.number_input("Price", value=10.0, key="price")
    qty = st.slider("Qty", 1, 10, 1)
    if qty > 5:
        st.warning("Bulk order")
    st.metric("Total", f"{price * qty:.2f}")

def test_total_and_warning():
    at = AppTest.from_function(app).run()
    assert at.metric[0].value == "10.00"
    assert len(at.warning) == 0
    at.slider[0].set_value(6).run()
    at.number_input(key="price").set_value(2.5).run()
    assert at.metric[0].value == "15.00"
    assert at.warning[0].value == "Bulk order"
    assert not at.exception

test_total_and_warning()
print("passed")                         # run with pytest in a real project
takeaways: AppTest runs apps headless: `AppTest.from_file('app.py').run()`
Inspect elements by type or key and interact with set_value, click, input, then `.run()`
Preset `session_state` and `secrets`; assert `not at.exception`
pitfalls: Forgetting to call `.run()` after interacting, so assertions see the previous state.

quiz.q: After `at.button[0].click()`, the assertions still see the old output. What is missing?
options: A call to .run() to rerun the script
quiz.explain: Interactions only queue new widget values; .run() executes the script with them.

concepts.name: Configuration, deployment and authentication
concepts.summary: Configure apps with config.toml, deploy to Community Cloud or containers, add OIDC login with st.login, and plan for scaling.
concepts.why: Shipping an app to real users raises questions of configuration, hosting, auth and capacity that the dev server hides.
concepts.body:
**Configuration** lives in `.streamlit/config.toml` (project) or `~/.streamlit/config.toml`, and every option can also be a CLI flag or an environment variable: `[server] port = 8080` equals `--server.port 8080` and `STREAMLIT_SERVER_PORT=8080`. `streamlit config show` lists all options. Common ones: `server.port`, `server.address`, `server.headless = true` (no browser), `server.maxUploadSize` (MB), `server.baseUrlPath` behind a proxy, `client.toolbarMode`, and a `[theme]` section (`primaryColor`, `base`, fonts).

**Hosting options**:

- Streamlit Community Cloud: connect a GitHub repo, set secrets in the UI.
- Containers: a Docker image running `streamlit run app.py --server.port=8501 --server.address=0.0.0.0`, with a health check on `/_stcore/health`.
- Snowflake, cloud platforms and Kubernetes. Recent versions also provide `st.App`, an ASGI application you can run with uvicorn or mount inside FastAPI or Starlette.

**Authentication**: `st.login()` starts an OpenID Connect flow (Google, Microsoft, Okta, Auth0 ...) configured under `[auth]` in secrets (redirect URI, cookie secret, client id and secret, metadata URL). Afterwards `st.user.is_logged_in` and `st.user` attributes such as email are available, and `st.logout()` ends the session.

**Scaling**: each user session holds a WebSocket and its session state in the server process, and runs reruns in threads. A single process serves many light users, but CPU-heavy reruns contend for the GIL. Scale out with several replicas behind a load balancer with **sticky sessions** (WebSocket affinity), share caches through external stores, and keep heavy computation in cached functions or background services.
concepts.code:
# .streamlit/config.toml
[server]
headless = true
port = 8501
maxUploadSize = 50          # MB
enableXsrfProtection = true

[theme]
base = "light"
primaryColor = "#E8383D"

# .streamlit/secrets.toml (excerpt) for st.login() with an OIDC provider
[auth]
redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/oauth2callback"
cookie_secret = "a-long-random-string"
client_id = "..."
client_secret = "..."
server_metadata_url = "https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration"

# Dockerfile essentials:
#   CMD ["streamlit", "run", "app.py", "--server.address=0.0.0.0"]
#   HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8501/_stcore/health
takeaways: Options come from config.toml, CLI flags or STREAMLIT_* environment variables
Deploy via Community Cloud, containers with `/_stcore/health`, or `st.App` under ASGI
`st.login` adds OIDC auth; scale out with sticky sessions and shared caches
pitfalls: Load balancing replicas without sticky sessions, which breaks the WebSocket connection to a user's session.

quiz.q: You run three Streamlit replicas behind a load balancer and users randomly lose their state. What is the likely cause?
options: The load balancer is not using sticky sessions, so requests reach replicas without the user's session
The health check path is wrong
quiz.explain: Session state lives in one server process; without affinity, a user's WebSocket may reconnect to another replica.

concepts.name: Architecture: sessions, threads and reruns
concepts.summary: Understand how the Streamlit server, sessions, script threads, widget IDs and caches interact, to debug subtle bugs and design scalable apps.
concepts.why: Stale state, cross-user leaks, lost widget values and threading errors all trace back to how Streamlit runs scripts.
concepts.body:
When a browser opens an app, it connects over a **WebSocket** to the Streamlit server (Starlette and uvicorn today). The server creates an **AppSession** per connection with its own session state and a **ScriptRunner** that executes your script in a separate thread.

Each run executes the script with `exec`. Every `st.*` call sends a **delta** (a protobuf message) describing an element; the front end applies deltas to the page in order. At the end of the run, elements not re-sent are removed. If a widget changes while a run is still executing, the current run is stopped at its next `st.*` call by an internal exception derived from `BaseException`, and a new run starts. A bare `except:` around `st` calls would swallow it; `except Exception` does not.

**Widget identity** is a hash of the widget type, its parameters and its `key`. Same ID across runs means the value is preserved; any parameter change creates a new widget with its default value. Widgets not rendered in a run are dropped from session state.

**Caches** are process-global, shared by all sessions and threads, so `cache_resource` objects must be thread-safe.

**Threads you create** do not have a script run context. Calling `st.*` from them fails or is ignored. Let such threads only compute and store results; display them from the script, for example in a fragment with `run_every`.

Globals in imported modules (unlike the main script, which is re-executed every run) are shared by all users; keep per-user data in session state.
concepts.code:
import threading, time
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_resource
def shared():                         # one dict per process, shared by ALL sessions
    return {"lock": threading.Lock(), "results": {}, "runs": 0}

def background_job(store, job_id):    # no st.* calls in this thread
    time.sleep(3)
    with store["lock"]:
        store["results"][job_id] = "done"

store = shared()
with store["lock"]:
    store["runs"] += 1                # counts every user's reruns
st.session_state.my_runs = st.session_state.get("my_runs", 0) + 1  # yours only

if st.button("Start job"):
    threading.Thread(target=background_job, args=(store, "job-1"), daemon=True).start()

@st.fragment(run_every="1s")          # poll from the script thread
def status():
    st.write("job-1:", store["results"].get("job-1", "running or not started"))
status()
st.caption(f"all runs={store['runs']}, my runs={st.session_state.my_runs}")
takeaways: Each tab is a session; its script runs in a thread and streams deltas over a WebSocket
Widget IDs derive from type, parameters and key; parameter changes reset widgets
Caches and imported-module globals are shared process-wide; session state is per user
pitfalls: Calling st.* functions from a background thread, which has no script run context.

quiz.q: You store the current user's cart in a global list inside a helper module the app imports. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; each user gets their own copy
All users share and modify the same cart
The list is cleared on every rerun
Streamlit raises an error at import
quiz.explain: Modules are imported once per process, so their globals are shared by every session.

concepts.name: Custom components
concepts.summary: Extend Streamlit with your own HTML, CSS and JavaScript using st.html and st.components.v2, exchanging data with Python.
concepts.why: When no built-in element or community component fits, a custom component adds any web UI to your app.
takeaways: `st.html` inserts static HTML/CSS without an iframe
`st.components.v2.component` registers HTML/CSS/JS with state and trigger values
Components are trusted code: escape anything user-provided
pitfalls: Interpolating user input or LLM output into a component's HTML, creating a cross-site scripting hole.

quiz.q: In a v2 component, which JavaScript call sends a one-off event (like a click) to Python rather than persistent state?
quiz.explain: Trigger values are transient events; state values persist across reruns.
